Gingerly

JIN-jer-lee -- of uncertain origin, possibly from Old French gençor ('more delicate'); NOT related to the spice ginger. · adverb

Hear It

What It Means

Gingerly is carefully and cautiously, especially when handling something fragile, painful, or risky.

Still favoring her sprained wrist, she gingerly lifted the heavy casserole dish out of the oven.

Worked Example

The technician gingerly lowered the antique clock's fragile glass face onto the workbench, aware that one wrong move could shatter it.

That slow, deliberate carefulness -- moving as if the object might break or the situation might go wrong -- is exactly what it means to do something gingerly.

How Gingerly Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

delicately

delicately: in a way that requires careful, gentle handling

warily

warily: in a watchful, cautious manner

Antonyms

recklessly

recklessly: without any care for consequences

carelessly

carelessly: without paying enough attention

How Strong Is It? — delicately → gingerly → warily

delicately vs. gingerly

delicately vs. gingerly: She delicately dusted the antique vase before placing it back on the shelf.

warily vs. gingerly

warily vs. gingerly: Warily is stronger than gingerly: you move gingerly when handling something fragile or painful, but a cat creeping warily around the vacuum is more intensely on guard, braced against real danger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Despite its look, gingerly has nothing to do with the spice ginger -- its true origin is uncertain, possibly tracing to an Old French word meaning 'delicate' or 'graceful.' Since there's no real productive root to build on, gingerly is best learned as its own word.

Use the root in a new word: ginger (unrelated!)

Use the root in a new word: ginger (unrelated!): Despite the resemblance, ginger the spice comes from an entirely different Sanskrit-rooted word -- it just happens to look and sound like gingerly.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Gingerly almost always describes a slow, careful physical action -- stepping, lifting, touching -- rather than a feeling. Don't confuse it with the unrelated spice ginger; the resemblance is a coincidence, not a shared root.
